# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium. Once considered a rare and untreatable disease, CA is increasingly recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), aortic stenosis, and arrhythmia [1,2]. Two protein precursors account for the overwhelming majority of cases: monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL amyloidosis) and transthyretin (ATTR amyloidosis), the latter subdivided into wild-type (ATTRwt) and hereditary (ATTRv) forms [3,4].

## Epidemiology and Pathophysiology

The true prevalence of CA has been historically underestimated. Autopsy studies and imaging-based screening have demonstrated ATTRwt deposits in up to 25% of elderly individuals and in a substantial proportion of patients with HFpEF and degenerative aortic stenosis [5,6]. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, with cardiac involvement portending the worst prognosis among systemic amyloidoses [7]. In ATTR amyloidosis, destabilization of the transthyretin tetramer leads to monomer dissociation, misfolding, and fibril formation; over 130 pathogenic TTR variants have been described, with the Val122Ile variant being especially common among individuals of African ancestry [8,9].

Amyloid infiltration causes progressive ventricular wall thickening, diastolic dysfunction, and ultimately restrictive physiology. Direct cytotoxicity from light chains contributes to the rapid clinical deterioration characteristic of AL cardiac disease [10].

## Clinical Presentation

CA should be suspected in patients with heart failure and increased left ventricular wall thickness in the absence of a hypertensive or valvular explanation [11]. Extracardiac clues include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, and autonomic dysfunction [12]. Low-voltage electrocardiograms disproportionate to wall thickness, conduction disease, and atrial arrhythmias are common [13]. AL amyloidosis may additionally present with nephrotic-range proteinuria, macroglossia, and periorbital purpura [7].

## Diagnosis

Echocardiography typically reveals concentric left ventricular thickening, biatrial enlargement, and impaired global longitudinal strain with characteristic apical sparing [14]. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrates diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement and elevated native T1 and extracellular volume [15,16].

A landmark advance has been the validation of bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy (technetium-99m pyrophosphate, DPD, or HMDP) for noninvasive diagnosis of ATTR-CA [17]. In the absence of a monoclonal protein, grade 2–3 myocardial uptake has a specificity and positive predictive value approaching 100% for ATTR-CA, obviating endomyocardial biopsy in many patients [18]. Crucially, exclusion of a plasma cell dyscrasia with serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light-chain assays is mandatory, since AL amyloidosis can also produce scintigraphic uptake [19]. Genetic testing distinguishes ATTRv from ATTRwt and informs family screening [9]. Endomyocardial biopsy with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry typing remains the gold standard when noninvasive findings are equivocal [20].

## Prognosis and Staging

Biomarker-based staging systems incorporating N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, troponin, and free light-chain differences predict survival in AL amyloidosis [21]. Analogous NT-proBNP– and renal-function–based staging systems stratify ATTR-CA [22]. Untreated AL-CA carries a median survival of less than six months once advanced heart failure develops, underscoring the need for prompt diagnosis [10].

## Treatment

Management of AL amyloidosis targets the underlying plasma cell clone. Daratumumab-based regimens combined with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone have improved hematologic and cardiac responses, as demonstrated in the ANDROMEDA trial [23]. Autologous stem cell transplantation benefits carefully selected patients [24].

For ATTR-CA, tafamidis, a transthyretin stabilizer, reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in the ATTR-ACT trial, becoming the first disease-modifying therapy approved for this condition [25]. Gene-silencing therapies, including the small interfering RNA agent patisiran and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen, were initially validated for hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy [26,27]. More recently, patisiran was evaluated in ATTR cardiomyopathy in the APOLLO-B trial [28]. CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing targeting hepatic TTR has shown durable serum transthyretin reduction in early-phase studies, representing a potentially transformative approach [29].

Supportive cardiac care emphasizes cautious diuresis; conventional heart-failure agents such as beta-blockers and renin-angiotensin inhibitors are frequently poorly tolerated owing to restrictive physiology and autonomic dysfunction [11]. Anticoagulation is warranted for atrial arrhythmias given the high thromboembolic risk [13].

## Conclusion

The landscape of cardiac amyloidosis has been transformed by noninvasive diagnostic algorithms and effective disease-modifying therapies [30]. Heightened clinical suspicion, particularly in elderly patients with unexplained ventricular thickening, HFpEF, or aortic stenosis, enables earlier diagnosis when therapy is most effective. Ongoing trials of gene-silencing and gene-editing agents promise further improvements in outcomes for this once-neglected disease.
